summary:
Project description (EN)

MarsWalk Planner is an offline simulator and planner for Mars surface walks. It combines a 3D map built on open NASA data with an onboard AI. The AI checks over 1,400 combinations of route, departure time and travel mode (on foot or by rover). It keeps a 30% oxygen reserve, never sends the crew out at night, and gives a clear GO or NO-GO with reasons. During the walk it watches oxygen. In danger it sounds an alarm and guides the crew by voice to the nearest base. The map also shows dust storms, radiation, water-bearing minerals and 10 Mars sites in 3D. The whole app is a single file that runs on any laptop or tablet with no internet, in Kazakh, Russian and English.

Idea (EN)

A signal from Mars takes up to 24 minutes to reach Earth, and sometimes there is no link for two weeks. If something goes wrong outside, Earth can’t help in time — the crew decides alone. We give astronauts an assistant on board: it checks the route in advance, explains every decision, and brings them home in an emergency. Today it’s a training tool for crews and education; tomorrow it’s an onboard system for Mars missions.
details:
Tools and technologies

  • App: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with raw WebGL2 for 3D rendering. No frameworks and no external requests.
  • Browser features: the Web Speech API for voice, the Web Audio API for alarms, and a service worker with a PWA manifest for offline use.
    • CTX DEM and orthomosaic for Jezero;
    • HRSC + MOLA DEM and Viking imagery for the other 9 sites;
    • MMGIS rover traverse;
    • CRISM minerals and AI4Mars terrain classes;
    • MDAD dust storm database;
    • REMS and MEDA weather;
    • MSL RAD radiation;
    • SWIM subsurface ice.
  • Development: we used the AI assistant Claude to help write code and texts.

What makes it creative

Most Mars maps are tools for scientists on Earth. MarsWalk turns open NASA datasets into a decision tool for the astronaut standing on Mars. It combines orbital data (terrain, minerals, storms) with rover data (weather, radiation, ground type) in one offline package. The AI does not just answer GO or NO-GO: it explains why. It also speaks to the crew in an emergency.

Factors we considered

  • Offline: the app must work with no internet or link to Earth.
  • Explainability: a life-or-death decision must be checkable.
  • Low workload: the interface stays simple for crews in suits.
  • Conservative margins: a 30% oxygen reserve and the walk-back rule.
  • Honest uncertainty: the app shows how old its data is, and orbital maps miss small rocks.
  • Ordinary hardware: any device that can open a web page.
  • Accessibility: three languages, voice alerts and an accessibility menu.
